task.goal: Test whether a classroom plant grows differently under two existing window positions.
hard_constraints: Twelve similar plants, six weeks, no growth chamber or extra lamps.
Do not change watering based on observed growth; log temperature and watering.
Avoid treating one plant as proof; define missing-plant and measurement rules before starting.
task.available_resources: Ruler, daily room thermometer and notebook.
task.expected_result: A controlled small experiment with cautious inference.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Matched-pair randomized comparison at the two windows
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use six matched pairs to estimate whether the two existing window positions produce different six-week height gains. Differences in light and local conditions could change growth; this experiment estimates their combined effect, not light alone.

Before assignment, measure all twelve plants and pair them by starting height and visible condition. Randomly assign one plant from each pair to each window using labeled notebook slips drawn without looking. Keep plants at their assigned window for six weeks. Randomize their order within each window initially, then cycle positions within that window on a fixed weekly schedule to distribute local shading.

This requires similar plants, preferably the same species, comparable existing pots and soil, sufficient space, and an existing way to deliver consistent water quantities. Prespecify the same watering quantity and schedule for every plant, based on ordinary care requirements; never adjust it in response to growth. Record every watering and any deviation. Log room temperature daily at a fixed time and location. A single room thermometer cannot establish simultaneous temperature differences between windows.

The main limitation is that there is only one example of each window position. Results apply to these plants at these windows during these six weeks; they cannot establish a general effect of window orientation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Before starting, define height as the vertical distance from the soil surface to the highest living growing point, measured without stretching the plant. Measure weekly at the same time of day, with the same ruler and observer. Record damage, death, and absence separately.

The primary outcome is each plant’s week-six height minus its baseline height. Compare the two gains within each original pair; report all six differences, their mean, and their range against the simple comparator of zero difference.

Prespecify no replacements or invented measurements. A missing baseline or final measurement excludes that pair from the primary paired comparison; retain its available records and report why it is incomplete. Report deaths separately, and call the primary comparison inconclusive if fewer than four complete pairs remain.

The smallest measurement check is to measure every plant twice at baseline, hiding the first readings. If repeat discrepancies are comparable to the eventual window difference, or pair differences have mixed directions, the evidence for a detectable height effect is weak. Height alone does not measure total plant health or biomass.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Weekly randomized window assignments
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Test whether a week at either window changes height growth by repeatedly randomizing exposure. Unlike keeping each plant at one window, this design lets plants experience both positions, reducing the influence of persistent differences between plants. It estimates the average short-term effect of the current window across differing exposure histories; it does not directly estimate six uninterrupted weeks at one window.

Label twelve similar plants. At the start of each of six weeks, independently draw six labels for window A; place the remaining six at window B. Record assignments before moving plants. Randomize spaces within each window and handle every pot equally, including plants staying at their previous window.

Use existing comparable pots and soil, a ruler, thermometer, notebook, and an existing means of giving consistent water quantities. Before starting, fix a common watering quantity and schedule appropriate for the plants. Log all watering and deviations; never adjust watering according to growth. Record room temperature at the same time and location daily. This cannot resolve temperature differences between windows.

The key uncertainty is response timing: plants may respond slowly or retain effects of earlier exposure. Consequently, a small weekly difference would not rule out a sustained window effect.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Before assignment, define height as soil surface to the highest living growing point without stretching. Measure at baseline and each weekly boundary, before moving plants, using the same observer, ruler, and time of day. Repeat baseline measurements with earlier readings hidden to assess measurement noise.

For each week, subtract starting height from ending height and compare mean gains at A and B. Average the six weekly contrasts, report each contrast and individual trajectories, and use zero difference as the comparator. Repeated observations are not 72 independent plants.

Prespecify no replacements or imputation. A missing endpoint makes that plant-week unavailable; record deaths separately. Declare the comparison inconclusive if fewer than four weeks retain at least four measurable plants per window. Report missingness by assignment because selective loss can bias results.

As a small diagnostic, compare contrasts among plants that switched windows with those that stayed. Opposing patterns suggest carryover or movement effects and weaken a simple current-window interpretation. Differences comparable to ruler repeatability also provide weak evidence.

EXPAND.title: Balanced crossover: let each plant experience both windows
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a three-week crossover to reduce the influence of persistent differences among plants. Each plant serves as its own comparison: growth during its time at window A is compared with growth during its time at window B. Unlike the prior fixed-window design, this can separate stable plant vigor from window response, but introduces carryover and moving effects.

A teacher owns the six-week trial. Label twelve similar plants of one species, measure starting heights, and randomly assign six to sequence A→B and six to B→A using notebook slips. At week three, exchange windows. Keep pots, soil, and care unchanged; prespecify placement within each window so plants do not shade one another systematically.

Use the ruler, notebook, daily thermometer, and an existing watering vessel capable of repeatable quantities. Before starting, specify a common watering amount and schedule suitable for the species; never adjust watering in response to growth. Log every watering, deviations, and daily temperature at a fixed room location and time. Room readings cannot establish window-specific temperatures.

This route assumes growth responds within three weeks and previous exposure has limited lasting effects. It estimates short-term response to these two positions, rather than the effect of six continuous weeks at either window.
EXPAND.experiment:
Before assignment, define height as soil surface to highest living growing point without stretching. Measure weekly with the same observer and ruler; repeat baseline readings to assess measurement disagreement.

For each plant, calculate three-week height gain at A minus gain at B. Report individual differences and the mean separately for each sequence, then average the two sequence means equally to balance calendar-period effects. Also report the first three weeks as a simple randomized parallel comparison.

Prespecify no replacements or interpolated heights. Missing baseline, week-three, or week-six measurements exclude that plant from the crossover calculation; retain other records and report deaths separately. Fewer than four complete plants per sequence makes the comparison inconclusive. End comparative inference if either position becomes unsafe; record any rescue care.

Check whether both sequence means favor the same window and exceed measurement disagreement. Compare this conclusion with the first-period parallel result, alongside deaths and damage following the move. Opposite sequence effects or reversal after switching would weaken the crossover interpretation. Agreement cannot prove improvement over the prior six-week fixed-window route, which is not concurrently tested.

EXPAND.title: Improved P0: matched-pair randomized comparison with prespecified measurement and missing-plant rules
EXPAND.proposal:
Retain P0’s mechanism: randomly assign one plant from each of six matched pairs to each window for six continuous weeks. Window conditions may change growth; pairing reduces starting differences. This estimates the combined effect of these particular positions, not light alone. The substantive improvement is to specify outcome, missing-data, and care rules before assignment, closing gaps in P0’s execution.

A teacher owns the trial. Label plants in the notebook using a placement map, measure starting height, and pair by height and visible condition. Randomly assign within pairs using folded notebook slips. Prespecify six spaces at each window and rotate plants among those spaces weekly, without changing windows.

Measure weekly from the soil surface to the main stem’s growing tip, with pots resting normally and without stretching stems. Record to the ruler’s smallest division. Immediately repeat each measurement; if readings differ by more than two divisions, take a third and record the median. Primary outcome is week-six minus starting height. This requires similar plants whose main stems can be measured meaningfully. If that prerequisite fails, use a prespecified count of fully opened leaves throughout, recording starting counts before randomization.

Use the same predetermined watering schedule and quantity for all twelve plants, based on their normal care requirements. This assumes existing access to water and a repeatable delivery method; the supplied ruler cannot itself measure water volume. If measured quantities are unavailable, prespecify identical delivery actions and log that limitation. Never change watering because of observed growth. Log every watering, deviations, and daily room temperature at a fixed place and time.

Do not replace missing or dead plants. Record dates and reasons; death is a separate outcome, not zero growth. Analyze available complete pairs, list every exclusion, and treat fewer than four complete pairs as insufficient for the planned growth comparison.
EXPAND.experiment:
Before assignment, inspect all twelve plants using duplicate measurements. Compare first readings with the repeated-reading summaries: fewer discrepancies relative to starting differences would support the added measurement procedure; unchanged readings show no observable gain, while added measurement time is its cost. Record that time.

At six weeks, report all pairwise growth differences, their mean and range, and losses by window. Compare the estimated window difference using first readings versus the prespecified summaries. Agreement supports robustness; disagreement exposes measurement sensitivity without establishing which estimate is correct. Stop at six weeks; end an individual plant’s participation for serious distress requiring care outside the protocol, record it, and provide normal care. With six pairs and one location of each type, small or inconsistent differences remain inconclusive.
